item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox are in the playoffs for the second straight year. The clinch became official Sunday when the Braves beat the Astros, guaranteeing Boston a spot in the Wild Card Series starting on September 29.
The roster is not yet complete. Several key arms are still working their way back from injuries, and the next six games at Fenway Park will determine how the pitching staff looks when October arrives.
One of the biggest names on that list took a step forward this week.
Tracy Provides Update on Crochet
Garrett Crochet is closing in on a significant milestone in his comeback. Interim manager Chad Tracy said the plan is for Crochet to throw a live bullpen session against hitters early next week, with Tuesday as the hopeful target.
"Maybe early next week, a potential IBP dependent on how he feels over the next couple days," Tracy said. "Maybe early next week we'll be able to face some hitters. But yeah, tentative."
Crochet's ramp-up has been deliberate at every stage, and the Red Sox are not going to rush the left-hander into a situation he is not ready for.
Facing live hitters would represent the most significant test of Crochet's rehab to this point. He threw 30 pitches over two simulated innings earlier this month, and Tracy said at the time that everything went well. A live session against hitters is the next level up.
What Crochet Would Mean for October
Crochet's potential availability changes the shape of Boston's postseason pitching plans.
The rotation is lining up with Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Ranger Suarez as the likely starters for the Wild Card Series. Tolle has posted a 2.44 ERA across his last eight starts. Gray has been one of the best starters in the American League this season, carrying a 2.76 ERA.
Adding Crochet would give Tracy another weapon to deploy, albeit from the bullpen.
Tyron Guerrero returned from the injured list Sunday and looked sharp. Aroldis Chapman, Garrett Whitlock, and Erik Miller round out a late-inning group that has carried the pitching staff down the stretch. Tanner Houck continues to progress through minor league rehab and remains a potential option.
Final Word for the Red Sox
Garrett Crochet is not back yet. The live bullpen is tentative. The timeline is still dependent on how his body responds day to day.
The Red Sox have been patient with this process, and that patience could pay off at exactly the right time.
Tuesday will tell the story. If Crochet gets through a live session clean, Boston's pitching picture for the postseason gets significantly deeper.

item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — Craig Breslow stood in a puddle of beer in his stocking feet on Sunday, watching the team he assembled celebrate having clinched its spot in the postseason.
That’s when he realized he still had his phone in his pocket. The Red Sox chief baseball officer carefully picked his way down the hallway to put it out of harm’s way before he got even more soaked.
“Smart move,” Breslow was told.
“It might be too late,” he said, laughing.
You can always get a new phone. But how often can you enjoy the satisfaction of proving that an entire city, if not an entire industry, was wrong?
Breslow made what still remains the most stunning move of this baseball season when he fired Alex Cora and six of his coaches on April 25 after only 27 games.
He was convinced the team had potential it would not realize under Cora and needed a change.
“I believed in the players that we had, and I felt it was really important that we acted definitively and decisively when we did, so that we could create an environment around the players that was supportive, that would allow them to thrive, and they responded,” he said.
“And, while there may have been some people that questioned what this group was capable of, I think they answered.”
Some people? How about most of us?
It was not a straight line to success. The Sox were 13-16 in the first 29 games under interim manager Chad Tracy, and I wrote in late May that it was time to start rebuilding by getting a jump on the trade deadline.
With Roman Anthony and Garrett Crochet on the injured list, it seemed obvious the Sox weren’t going to contend. There were loud “sell the team” chants at Fenway Park.
Tracy’s record was 22-29 three weeks later, and even the players had started to question what was going on at Fenway Park.
“We’re not good. We’re just not a good team right now. That’s just a fact,” righthander Sonny Gray said after a 3-2 loss against the Blue Jays on June 18.
I wrote the next day that it felt inevitable the Sox would be sellers and could well finish the season with 95 losses. Some executives from other teams believed Breslow could only save his job by turning veterans into prospects.
You know what happened next. The Sox went on a season-saving 32-6 run and are now a threat to make a deep run into October. They are the first team in history to lose 44 of their first 75 games and make the playoffs.
“You stared impossible in the face with the position we were in,” Tracy told his players on Sunday.
Breslow did not see any particular series or moment as a turning point.
“I think the turnaround was the result of incremental change, incremental improvement, changes to the way that we practice, the ways that we trained, the way that we delivered information to our players, the way that we supported our players,” he said.
“So I think when you put all those things together, they compound, and then ultimately the performance on the field by way of wins and losses was the last thing to catch up.”
Breslow spent 12 seasons pitching in the majors and grew a beard with the rest of the wild bunch Red Sox of 2013. He appeared in 10 of the 16 playoff games that season and got three huge outs in the eighth inning of Game 6 in the ALCS.
His job now is giving others that opportunity. But in the end, you’re standing in the same puddle of beer with a big smile.
“The obvious difference is I didn’t have a direct impact on the outcomes of games in this role, whereas I did as a player,” Breslow said. “But I think there’s a different sense of gratification when you’re kind of part of this massive effort to identify players and bring them in and help support the coaching staff.
“It’s very different, and in some ways it’s maybe a couple of layers removed. But it’s certainly as satisfying.”
Breslow has earned that satisfaction. The job’s not over, but he had it right about this team.

As the clinch celebration played out in the Tropicana Field visitors’ clubhouse early Sunday evening, the incompleteness of the moment was not lost on the revelling Boston Red Sox.
The achievement was dampened, and not only in the literal sense by the champagne with which the Red Sox doused each other and the room. That they had lost the series to the Tampa Bay Rays barely an hour earlier and instead had their ticket punched via an Atlanta Braves victory over the Houston Astros. The Red Sox are 9-9 this month, struggling offensively, without on several injured stars, and are their first postseason round will almost certainly be a rematch of last year’s best-of-three Wild Card series at Yankee Stadium, where they fell to their rivals 2-1.
In other words, there is much work to be done. The Red Sox know it, and they are eager to prove they did not come this far to only go this far.
“This has been a turbulent season,” Red Sox chief baseball officer Craig Breslow told reporters. “This is certainly an accomplishment, but it’s not the primary objective here.”
But neither the recent struggles nor the battles ahead should diminish the magnitude of the overall achievement of getting to this point.
The Red Sox lost American League Cy Young runner-up Garrett Crochet to a shoulder injury in mid-April, and he has yet to return.
They fired manager Alex Cora and several coaches in the middle of a late-April road series in Baltimore, and promoted Triple-A Worcester skipper Chad Tracy and several others from their minor league coaching ranks.
Injuries sidelined star outfielder Roman Anthony and veteran shortstop Trevor Story from early May until the very end of August.
The Red Sox owned their worst home record to start a season since 1932, and were 15 1/2 games out of first in the American League East in June.
On June 24, they fell to 14 games under .500. On Sunday, they became the fourth team in Major League Baseball history to go from as many as 14 games under .500 to the postseason in the same season.
“We needed time, and the time came for us,” veteran first baseman Willson Contreras told his teammates in the clubhouse. “I’m very proud of you all.”
“It’s 162 for a reason,” echoed third baseman Caleb Durbin.
“Obviously, getting where we want to go, but ultimately, what we had to overcome to get here makes it all the more sweet,” Tracy said. “We had a long way to go, and they never stopped, and they didn’t take no for an answer.”
This year looked lost, and the Red Sox managed to save it. They maintained an unshakeable belief in themselves, and it has already taken them to places most of the baseball world doubted it could go.
“Belief, belief, belief,” Contreras told reporters. “That was my main word, and that’s what I did from Day 1.”
The Red Sox are not a perfect team. But they certainly have the grit and gumption to go further than expected, as evidenced by the fact that they have already done so by reaching this point.
“We know how it felt when we left New York at the end of the year,” Story said. “You know how it made me feel. So that stayed with me.”
“They came together, and they found a way to get it done, and they had a long way to go to do it,” Tracy said. “They’re very battle-tested, and I’m super, super proud of them.”
“We don’t care where we play,” Tracy said. “You go back to July, and most people didn’t think we’d even be standing here. So it doesn’t matter where we play.”
“We’re in,” Tracy continued. “You got a ticket to the dance, and now you got to go take care of it there.”
“We’re in, baby,” Story said. “Let’s go.”
“Now, this is the moment,” right-fielder Wilyer Abreu said, “that we (were) waiting for.”

Garrett Whitlock is looking to make a career pivot and transition into the starting rotation. For the Boston Red Sox, it's a strange proposition. The right-hander is one of the best setup men in the league, and that has tremendous value.
Of course, starting pitchers have even more value, hence the higher salaries, but the transition is a risk. Not only does a hurler need to reserve something in the tank rather than just air it out for an inning, but he also needs to have enough variation in his arsenal to turn over a lineup multiple times.
Some Red Sox beat writers don't believe the transition is the best idea. The biggest concern is whether or not Whitlock's health can hold up under a starter's workload. The 30-year-old's past forays into starting have resulted in injuries, making this a serious concern and not just some folks crying wolf.
However, there are still reasons to give it a try. Not now, of course. But in 2027, Whitlock in the rotation could make a lot of sense for a few distinct reasons.
The Red Sox should roll the dice on Garrett Whitlock as a starter in 2027
Presumably, the reason Whitlock would like to try his hand again in the rotation is monetary. On the free-agent market, mid-rotation starters can get upwards of $15 million per season. Look at guys like Chris Bassit and Merrill Kelly, for example, who are making $18.5 million and $18 million this season, respectively.
However, Boston holds options for 2027 and 2028 on Whitlock. If exercised, the Red Sox will pay him $8.25 million next year and $10.5 million in 2028. If he works out as a starter, that's an incredible value.
The next reason to give this a go is the fact that Whitlock has the repertoire to work in the rotation. While the majority of relievers are one-or-two-pitch pitchers, Whitlock has three quality offerings. His sinker is the cornerstone, which he throws 56% of the time, but he has a slider and changeup, too.
The slider he uses at a 26% rate, and it generates a ton of whiffs, coming in at 46.7%. The change gets broken out at an 18% clip, is a weapon against lefties, and also has a healthy 35.6% whiff rate. You might like to see a fourth pitch, just to have a show-me offering, but that's a solid foundation for a starter.
The next point is about righty-lefty balance. The Red Sox have an extreme imbalance towards southpaws. Theoretically, if everyone is healthy, you have Garrett Crochet, Ranger Suarez, Payton Tolle, and Jake Bennett all throwing from the left side. If Sonny Gray retires, Boston will have to find a righty to avoid skewing entirely left-handed.
Finally, the risk is minimal. As long as he doesn't suffer a catastrophic injury, the Red Sox can always stick Whitlock back in the bullpen and have a dominant high-leverage reliever should he struggle as a starter. In that regard, they're playing with house money. They control his future for the next two years, and he's paid a reasonable rate for a setup man, and what would be a steal for a No. 3 or No. 4 starter. At that point, why not take the plunge?

ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — The Red Sox will start Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Ranger Suarez in the series against the Guardians that starts Tuesday at Fenway Park.
That would conceivably line them up for the Wild Card Series that starts on Sept. 29 with six days rest each.
“Don’t read into that yet,” interim manager Chad Tracy said Sunday before a 5-1 loss against the Rays. “We can line that up still however we want.”
True. But Tolle has a 2.44 ERA in his last eight starts. He also has faced the Yankees twice this season and allowed one run on four hits over 13 innings with three walks and 18 strikeouts.
Gray allowed three runs on nine hits over 13⅔ innings in two starts against the Yankees. He struck out 12 and walked three.
Guerrero returns
Righthanded reliever Tyron Guerrero returned from a 19-day stint on the injured list with shoulder inflammation. Righthanded reliever Wyatt Olds was optioned to Triple-A Worcester.
Guerrero pitched a perfect eighth inning, striking out two.
“Felt good to be out there,” Guerrero said. “If I get a few more games I’ll be fine [for the postseason].”
Guerrero, 35, was called up in May for his first major league stint since 2019. He emerged as a reliable late-inning option, posting a 3.18 ERA over 39 games.
“He’s obviously a very important piece to this puzzle in our bullpen,” Tracy said.
Olds deserved a better fate. The 27-year-old has a 1.20 ERA and 1.20 WHIP in 13 games since making his major league debut on Aug. 17.
“Very tough. He’s thrown the ball great. He’s got big stuff,” Tracy said. “We had to make a roster decision.”
Contreras doing better
Willson Contreras took some swings in the batting cage to test his bruised right hand and came through fine. He said he hopes to be able to do more on Tuesday. “Step in the right direction,” Tracy said … There was no update on Garrett Crochet, who has yet to face hitters. That could come in the next few days … Tanner Houck had a 3.38 ERA over eight innings in four minor league games. Tracy suggested he would face hitters in a simulated game early this week. “Figuring out the next steps at home — and want to figure that out — but no plans for the next outing,” Tracy said. Could Houck be activated? “It’s possible,” Tracy said. “At this point, it’s going to depend very much on where’s the roster at, what are the needs, and then go from there.”… Rays shortstop Taylor Walls showed his baseball acumen in the first inning. With Roman Anthony on first and one out, he allowed Adley Rutschman’s popup to drop. Walls picked up the ball and flipped to second to get the force on Anthony. That left the Sox with a slower runner on first. It ultimately didn’t matter as Trevor Story struck out … Worcester, as Double-A Portland also did last weekend, had its final game rained out. The WooSox finished 76-67. Kutter Crawford was at Polar Park, and the plan was to have him start what would have been a bullpen game. Crawford has not appeared in a major league game since Sept. 28, 2024. He missed the 2025 season because of an injured right knee. He injured his right wrist in August of that season doing yard work at his home in Florida. Crawford pitched three innings in a rehab game for Worcester on April 11 but had a setback and wasn’t cleared for a game until Sunday. “He got to a point where he wanted to go out there and throw one,” Tracy said.

Not long after, the Braves beat the Astros, officially punching Boston’s ticket to the playoffs as one of the AL’s three Wild Card teams.
It’s a postseason appearance few saw coming when the Sox started the season 32-46. Not only are they the first team in history to advance to finish above .500 after losing as many as 32 of their first 78 games, but now they have a postseason berth to go with it.
Currently sitting as the No. 5 seed, the Red Sox are most likely to open their playoff run with a best-of-three Wild Card Series at Yankee Stadium, starting on Sept. 29. It would be a rematch from last year, when the Yankees won in three games after the Sox had taken the opener behind a brilliant performance by Garrett Crochet.
In a bit of baseball poetry, a home run swing from Mike Yastrzemski, the grandson of Red Sox legend Carl, gave the Braves a lead they would not relinquish and helped officially push Boston into the postseason.
“When you work as hard as we have worked, it was almost July [before we got going], and to fight as hard as we did, to put ourselves in the position we did, I don’t think you care much how it gets done,” said interim manager Chad Tracy, who took over after the dismissal of Alex Cora on April 25. “You just want to see your ticket get punched.”
For several weeks, the Red Sox never stopped punching. The road back to contention started with a four-game sweep of the Yankees at Fenway from June 25-28.
It continued on July 3, when the Sox began what would become a winning streak of 15 games, tying the franchise record set by the 1946 pennant winners of Ted Williams, Bobby Doerr, Dom DiMaggio and Johnny Pesky.
And even after that streak was snapped, the Sox shortly thereafter ripped off another nine-game winning streak, giving them the best 30-game stretch in team history. Including the Yankees sweep that started it all, Boston was 32-5 from June 25-Aug. 7.
Just when the rabid fanbase known as Red Sox Nation thought they were losing their summer, Boston pulled off one of the most remarkable turnarounds in history, and got the first reward for that on Sunday.

The Boston Red Sox are just a few wins from clinching a playoff spot for the second year in a row following a three-year hiatus. It's been a successful year on paper for the Red Sox, especially given all of their early-season chaos. But it's hard not to wonder... what if this team had been healthier in 2026?
Deadline acquisition Curtis Mead barely got to play at all for the Red Sox, and now he could be done for the season. Garrett Crochet made just six starts for Boston. Roman Anthony lost the bulk of what was supposed to be his first full MLB season. Justin Slaten's season is now over prematurely.
Everywhere you look on Boston's '26 roster, there are questions about what could have been. Mead is a potent right-handed bat who was supposed to add not only extra thump to the lineup but also infield depth.
Crochet is a much bigger theoretical. Last year's AL Cy Young runner-up pitched just 30 innings for Boston this season before landing on the IL with shoulder inflammation. In essence, the Red Sox rotation has been missing its true ace for nearly the entire year.
Red Sox's 2026 season comes with a huge "What if?"
Anthony’s absence was also tough to swallow for months. He hit .292/.396/.463 with an 140 OPS+ in 71 games as a 21-year-old in 2025, leading many to crown him Boston's franchise player moving forward. This year he played 30 games, then tore a ligament in his right ring finger on a check swing in early May. It was a freak injury that a hand specialist told reporters he had never seen isolated that way.
The Red Sox couldn't have expected Anthony to miss as much time as he did, and the somewhat mysterious nature of the injury made it impossible to plan for when he'd come back. It was a perpetual "when's he coming back?" buzzkill situation for the organization and its fans for months, not that Anthony is to blame.
Anthony and Crochet's absences alone make one wonder if the Red Sox would have already clinched by now had those two been healthy for most of the season. Certainly the Wild Card, no? The division is a harder argument, based on how good Tampa Bay has been all year. But we can realistically assume that the Red Sox would at least be battling the Yankees for the wild-card lead right now (or better) had Anthony and Crochet played more games.
Alas, that's all water under the bridge, and this roster is still on track for October baseball, thanks to a historic surge after the All-Star break. This is a more patched-together version of the Red Sox than any Boston fan would have preferred, but such is often the consequence of a 162-game marathon. Even so, no matter how Boston fares in the postseason (outside of a run to the World Series), fans will always be asking "What if?" about this year.

The Boston Red Sox will face off against the Tampa Bay Rays on Sunday in a rubber match on the road and the Red Sox got a reinforcement back just in time for the series finale.
Boston has been missing 2026 breakout flamethrower Tyron Guerrero since Aug. 31. That will change on Sunday afternoon. The Red Sox announced that Guerrero is back and righty Wyatt Olds has been sent down to Triple-A in response.
"The Red Sox today reinstated RHP Tyron Guerrero from the 15-Day Injured List. To make room, Boston optioned RHP Wyatt Olds to Triple-A Worcester," the Red Sox announced.
The Red Sox Got A Key Back
Over the last few weeks, much has been said about the reinforcements coming. Guerrero's return is the first example of this. The 6'8'' righty has a 3.26 ERA and a 36-to-7 strikeout-to-walk ratio in 38 2/3 innings pitched. It had been seven years since Guerrero had pitched in a big league game before the 2026 season. He last pitched in the majors back in 2019 with the Miami Marlins. He's been a breakout story for the Red Sox and now he's back.
Olds has been very good when he has been active on the big league roster this season. He has a 1.20 ERA in 13 appearances this season as a rookie, to go along with a 20-to-7 strikeout-to-walk ratio in 15 innings pitched.
Guerrero is the first reinforcement back for the bullpen, but he isn't likely to be the last. Garrett Crochet and Tanner Houck are two other guys who could be back in the not-so-distant future. Houck is closer than Crochet is. Houck has been on a minor league rehab assignment. Crochet has been tossing bullpens, but hasn't advanced to facing live hitters just yet.
Olds has been good, but it was known that difficult bullpen decisions would be coming. This is the first and we should see more in the coming days.
Guerrero went from unknown among the Red Sox's fanbase, to a high-leverage guy for Boston fairly quickly. Now, he's back as Boston has a chance to clinch a spot in the postseason on Sunday afternoon against the Rays. If the Red Sox take down Tampa Bay, they will officially punch their ticket. Boston's magic number is down to one. A win will get them into the playoffs. Even if they lose, they can make it in on Sunday with losses by other clubs fighting for the Wild Card spots. It could be a big day for Boston and Guerrero's back.

Curtis Mead has arguably been the most frustrating non-factor for the Boston Red Sox this season, because he never got his chance to make an impact.
In his very first game after being acquired in a trade with the Washington Nationals, Mead fractured his left wrist on a high-and-tight fastball against the Athletics. He quickly found himself in an uphill battle to return to action before the Red Sox's season ended at some point in the playoffs, but he's started making some progress.
According to a Saturday MLB.com injury update, Mead has begun hitting off a tee, which slipped under the radar amid a slough of injury news about Willson Contreras, Garrett Crochet, and others. Good news, to be sure, but far from a guarantee he makes it back for a game this year.
Mead's return not imminent, but progress made
Interim manager Chad Tracy said earlier this week that the tee work was beginning on Wednesday, per Boston Sports Gordo on X. That means we're a few days late to this particular story, so apologies to our readers — but not much slips by us, so it was a particularly quiet announcement.
Mead's breakout season (.851 OPS, 17 home runs in 88 games) was halted at the worst possible time. The Red Sox were looking to add an impact bat at the trade deadline, and Mead's absence has been nearly as awkward as Adley Rutschman's struggles.
Would Mead be the slam-dunk starter at second base even if he came back fully healthy this week? That's another real issue to consider, since Nick Sogard has done a nice job over the last month-plus. Perhaps Mead would at least be in the lineup against left-handed pitchers over the struggling Andruw Monasterio and/or Isiah Kiner-Falefa.
The Red Sox will have interesting decisions to make at the fringes of the roster for the first couple of rounds of the playoffs, no matter what. If Mead re-enters the picture, we could see someone who feels like they earned their spot get the axe, but that's the cost of doing business in a year when the American League could be up for grabs.

It’s the game of baseball, there’s ebbs and flows,” said Chad Tracy. “He came off the rehab, and for like five games, he looked fantastic. The Boston Red Sox are hoping to get one of their key bats back before the calendar flips to October.
Contreras' Injury and Recovery Timeline
Willson Contreras has been dealing with a hand injury after getting hit by a pitch on his right hand earlier in the week in Texas, an injury that's still visibly swollen and bruised days later. According to Peter Abraham of the Boston Globe, Contreras showed reporters the spot on his knuckles where the pitch connected. "When I got hit, I felt my hand going numb. I thought it was bad because that's a sign of a fracture," Contreras said. "That's why I came off the game."
Initial X-rays came back negative, though further imaging is being held off until the swelling subsides. Contreras sounds confident there's no fracture, drawing on past experience with broken bones to gauge the severity this time around.
The first baseman is hoping to take swings as soon as Sunday, though the nature of the injury complicates things given it's on his top hand, the one that absorbs the shock of contact. He's even considered wearing a protective guard over his batting glove if he does return. With Boston off Monday and playing the Rays again Sunday, Tuesday's game against the Guardians looks like the most realistic target for a potential comeback. "I'm going to take it day-to-day. Of course I want to come back and play with the guys and be there for them," Contreras said. "It's a part of baseball."
Contreras has now been hit by a pitch 24 times this season, tied for third-most in the majors, and 47 times across the last two seasons combined. Much of that stems from how close he stands to the plate, and he's voiced frustration about the pattern, at one point suggesting Boston's pitching staff should retaliate on his behalf.
Willson Contreras has more range of motion when he squeezes his hand today than he did yesterday. It remains a day to day monitoring for improvement. He is fairly confident it isn't fractured. He will do everything he can to play through this once symptoms allow.
— Ian Browne (@IanMBrowne) September 19, 2026
Other Red Sox Injury News
Contreras isn't the only Red Sox player working his way back. Center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela has been out since Sept. 3 with a strained right quadriceps. He faced live pitching for the first time since the injury during a Saturday workout in Worcester. "I felt comfortable," Rafaela said. He still needs to test a full-effort sprint before he's cleared. He plans to attempt that Sunday, with a possible return targeted for Tuesday against Cleveland.
On the pitching side, Tanner Houck continued his rehab from elbow surgery. He worked 3.1 innings in a minor league outing that included two strikeouts and no walks. It was his fourth appearance in that process. He could factor into Boston's bullpen plans for the postseason. Left-hander Garrett Crochet hasn't pitched since April 25 due to shoulder inflammation. He's targeting live hitters early this week, likely at Fenway Park. Whether that's enough to earn a postseason roster spot remains unclear. Right-handed reliever Tyron Guerrero could be activated as soon as Sunday after being out since Sept. 1 with a sore shoulder.

The Boston Red Sox got another promising day from lefty ace Garrett Crochet on Saturday on his quest back to the big leagues before the 2026 season comes to an end.
Crochet hasn't pitched in a game since April 25 due to shoulder/lat injuries. Since then, he has been working his way back and recently has been throwing bullpens. On Saturday, he tossed his latest over in Worcester at Polar Park. Crochet tossed about 20 pitches and reached 92 miles per hour. On top of this, WooSox pitching coach Dan DeLucia gave Boston fans some hope by saying he looked "great," as shared by Tommy Cassell of the Worcester Telegram and Gazette.
"Crochet, dressed in a full white Red Sox uniform, tossed roughly 20 pitches and sat in the 91 to 92 MPH range," Cassell wrote. "'He looks great,' DeLucia said. 'It was pretty much what we expected. Like, that was the expectation, go out there and kind of make it an in-between side start. No, actually probably a tick above what I think the expectations were, but for the most part, as expected the fine-tuning things, getting on the mound again.'"
The Red Sox Got Another Positive Day From Garrett Crochet
So, what should Red Sox fans make of this?
This is yet another positive. At first glance, the 91/92 MPH fastball may jump out to fans. Of course, that's not up to his peak and is approaching 100 MPH. But that's okay. The fact that DeLucia commented on the throwing session and even said that it was "probably a tick" above what they expected is a sign that he's continuing to make the progress the club has hoped for.
When it comes to Crochet, he has been throwing bullpens for weeks at this point. Earlier in the week, he advanced to a multi-inning up-and-down his last time out. The big lefty followed up on Saturday with a lighter workload. Earlier in the week he got up to 30 pitches and followed with another 20, or so, on Saturday.
For Crochet, the biggest thing to watch next will be when he faces live hitters. Facing live batters is the next big step. When he advances to that level, we'll start to get a real view of how he stacks up and whether he truly looks like himself. The current expectation is that a live bullpen will come early next week. The clock is ticking as well. There are just seven games left in the regular season. The playoffs will begin on Sep. 29. Will Crochet be ready by then? It's still possible.

item.content:encoded:
Can you believe the playoffs are almost here? A week from today the Red Sox will wrap up their regular season, closing the book on what has been among the most unexpected, topsy turvy seasons we’ve ever seen. From there the playoffs await, and who knows what twists and turns may still be in store.
But before we get there, what business is there left for the Red Sox to get squared away before Game 1 of the Wild Card series? We answer your questions in today’s Red Sox mailbag.
Tanner Houck and Garrett Crochet both appear close to ready to return. What is the chance that the Red Sox decide to put both of them on the postseason roster? Each feels like a high upside question mark but is it too risky relying on both of them to excel in limited roles? — Paul from Bluesky
If the Red Sox decide they’re ready I think there’s a great chance both pitch in the playoffs. The question of whether or not it’s too risky is valid, but the other factor to consider is would it be riskier to let an inferior arm take the mound at Yankee Stadium with the season on the line.
The nature of a best-of-three playoff series compared to a best-of-five or even a best-of-seven also makes the idea of loading up on short-inning relievers more attractive.
The Red Sox will only need three starting pitchers in the first round, presumably Sonny Gray, Ranger Suarez and Payton Tolle, in some order. That effectively frees up two additional bullpen spots, one of which I’m guessing will be filled by Jake Bennett as an emergency bulk man should the starter exit early due to injury or poor performance.
The back end of the bullpen is pretty much set in stone. If everyone is healthy and available it will be Aroldis Chapman, Garrett Whitlock, Erik Miller and Tyron Guerrero locking down the high leverage innings. But after that the Red Sox have some interesting decisions to make.
In one group you have the other short men, including Greg Weissert, Jovani Moran and Wyatt Olds. Then in the next group you have the longer men, including Patrick Sandoval, Brayan Bello, Alec Gamboa and Raymond Burgos. Finally, you have Crochet, Houck and Johan Oviedo, who has also begun a rehab assignment after missing nearly the entire season. What the Red Sox have to decide is which five of those 10 options give you the best chance to win?
I don’t think you can dispute that Crochet and Houck have the highest ceiling of that bunch, so if they’re good to go I don’t think the Red Sox will hesitate to give them the nod.
With Romy Gonzalez now hitting so well in Worcester, do you see him being put on the postseason roster as a lefty masher, and one of Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Andruw Monasterio or Jahmai Jones being left off? — @wcbosox on Bluesky
If the Red Sox believe Romy Gonzalez gives them the best chance to win in October, I feel like it would make sense for them to call him up and get him some looks at big league pitching over the last two weeks. You could make a great case that they should — he was batting .360 in 23 games since being optioned to Triple-A entering Friday — but if that doesn’t happen then that could be a sign the Red Sox don’t see him as part of the October plan.
Either way, the club has some tough decisions to make as far as constructing the bench goes.
Presuming that Ceddanne Rafaela returns from the IL without any issues and Willson Contreras isn’t sidelined by his hand injury, the Red Sox should enter the playoffs with a starting lineup featuring Adley Rutschman at catcher, Contreras, Nick Sogard, Trevor Story and Caleb Durbin across the infield, and an outfield of Rafaela, Wilyer Abreu, Roman Anthony and Jarren Duran, with one of Anthony or Duran presumably starting at designated hitter if a righty is on the mound.
That leaves four spots for Kiner-Falefa, Monasterio, Jones, Mickey Gasper, Connor Wong, Nate Eaton, Gonzalez and possibly Curtis Mead. For our purposes we can probably set aside Eaton, who will likely be optioned upon Rafaela’s activation, as well as Mead, who only just started swinging a light bat and won’t have the benefit of a rehab assignment prior to his return.
Let’s also set aside some of the more outside the box candidates like Braiden Ward, who has never appeared in a big league game but who may garner consideration as a late-inning pinch runner after stealing 60 bases at Triple-A.
One spot will go to a backup catcher, and while you could talk yourself into Gasper filling that role, Wong has the most familiarity with the pitching staff and the Red Sox would probably rather keep Gasper available as a pinch hitter without worrying about catching logistics.
How about the other three spots? Kiner-Falefa, Monasterio and Gonzalez are all versatile infield defenders who bat right-handed, so there’s some redundancy there. Jones also bats right-handed and could function as an emergency reserve outfielder in addition to his pinch hitter, and while Gasper is technically a switch hitter, his real value comes from the left side, where he’s crushed righties over the past month.
What’s going to happen? My guess is the bench will be Wong, Gasper, Jones and one of the three righty infielders. So to go back to your original question, could Gonzalez make the playoff roster over one of Kiner-Falefa, Monasterio or Jones? Yes, and in fact even if he doesn’t make the roster one of those guys could still wind up on the outside looking in.
If the playoffs started today who would be the starting second baseman? Also, what’s the long-term plan for that position? — Tom P.
If the playoffs started today I think Nick Sogard would be the clear choice to start at second base. He’s been an everyday player for the Red Sox since the end of July, and at a time where most of the offense has hit a skid Sogard has been a reliable contributor at the plate, batting .262 with five home runs and a .772 OPS entering the weekend since being called back up on July 29.
Long-term, the Red Sox have a couple of different candidates who could emerge in the coming years.
If he hadn’t broken his wrist in his team debut I think it’s safe to say Curtis Mead would have spent the past two months starting at second for the Red Sox. Prior to the trade he was in the midst of a breakout season with the Washington Nationals, and at only 25 years old there’s good reason to believe his best years are still ahead of him. Whether he returns in the playoffs or for the start of next season, Mead should have the best chance to claim second base for himself.
But outside of him, Sogard and perhaps Gonzalez or Anthony Seigler, there is one other wild card. That’s Franklin Arias.
The top Red Sox prospect is putting the finishing touches on a brilliant season, and if he continues to develop he should have a great chance of becoming a key building block, perhaps as soon as next year. With Story under contract for only one more season he will have an opportunity to slide right into the starting shortstop job entering 2028, but what if he proves he’s ready for primetime before that? In that case Arias might get an initial look at second, with Mead perhaps rotating between the designated hitter spot and occasionally giving Durbin and Contreras a breather at their corner infield positions.
Does MLB need to readjust its postseason schedule? The No. 2 or 3 team in the American League will be eliminated in a three-game series, meanwhile two teams that are barely .500 play each other in the first round. — Brandon C.
I like the idea that there should be a reward for winning your division. If you’re one of the top two division winners you get a first round bye, and if you’re the third division winner you at least get to host the best-of-three Wild Card series. I’m fine with that, even in a weird year like this where all of the American League’s best teams are in the same division and the other division leaders are mediocre at best.
But the problem is what happens afterwards. Like you said, the No. 2 and 3 teams in the AL are probably going to wind up being the Yankees and Red Sox, and whichever of those teams advances will have to play the No. 1 seeded Tampa Bay Rays. Meanwhile, all three teams on the other side of the bracket could potentially finish with worse records than anyone on the AL East side, and one of those clubs will be guaranteed a trip to the ALCS.
I think MLB could address this by reseeding after the Wild Card round. The top two division winners would still get home field advantage in their divisional series, but whichever team advancing out of the Wild Card round has the better record would be paired with the second division winner. So this year if the Red Sox beat the Yankees and let’s say the AL West champion wins their Wild Card series, the Red Sox would go on to play the AL Central champion instead of the Rays, while the AL West champion would get Tampa Bay even though they would have technically started the playoffs as the higher seed.
Most years it probably won’t make a huge difference, but reseeding ahead of the divisional round would strike a balance between preserving the incentives for winning your division while ensuring the bracket doesn’t become unbalanced.

There were many questions the New York Yankees needed Spencer Jones to answer this season. Now, we've seen enough of him, even if it's been in a couple of disjointed stints, to get a good idea of who he is at the major league level.
The answer: pretty damn good. After struggling early, Jones has found his footing. A big reason for his ascendancy has been surprising. The Vanderbilt product has mashed left-handed pitching.
He's now logged 51 plate appearances against lefties and has slashed an eye-watering .435/.490/.761 following his homer off Minnesota Twins lefty specialist Taylor Rodgers on Sept. 15. It was the first dinger Rodgers gave up to a left-handed hitter over 133 plate appearances this season.
The sample size isn't huge, but it's relatively significant. For example, Ben Rice has 209 plate appearances against lefties out of his 622 plate appearances. For Jones, the 51 matchups against southpaws are a decent portion of his 255 total plate appearances.
One of the most impressive things about how he's performed against same-handed pitching is the amount of power he's demonstrated. Obviously, the six-foot-seven outfielder is a behemoth, but most lefties, even those who perform well against southpaws, see a drop in power in those situations. Take Rice, for instance; his slugging percentage drops from .561 against righties to .457 against left-handers. That hasn't been the case for Jones.
This has just been one part of Jones' maturation process that should have every fan feeling confident about not only his future, but his ability to contribute now.
Spencer Jones' performance against lefties has Yankees well-positioned for playoffs vs. Red Sox
Overall, Jones is hitting .259/.331/.452 with 10 homers on the season. He's been even better since being recalled on July 22, posting a .271/.337/.490 line with eight of his 10 homers coming during this most recent span.
There should be no more doubt that he should start over Trent Grisham, assuming Grisham is healthy, once the playoffs roll around. A significant part of that reasoning has to do with his performance against southpaws.
Jones has learned a lot from Cody Bellinger on how to handle those tough at-bats since he's been up in the bigs and the star left fielder has been healthy.
“When we are in the dugout, he’s one of those people I can go up to and ask, like, ‘Yo, what did you see?’ He’ll tell me bluntly what he saw, how he saw it, and essentially what he’s going to do next time. It’s like, all right, good to know before I go even into my first (at-bat) what this MVP is going to do for his first at-bat. It’s pretty sweet knowing that I’ve got these guys to help me out,” Jones said to The Athletic this week.
He couldn't have a better mentor. Bellinger isn't hitting lefties as much as he did last year, when he put up an insane .353/.415/.601 line, but his .287/.346/.449 performance in 2026 is plenty good, and better than what he's done against righties. In fact, Bellinger is about as balanced as they come with an .804 career OPS against left-handers and an .819 mark against righties.
We spoke about Rice earlier, but the early-season drama about his usage against lefties is a thing of the past. While he has more pop against righties, Rice's .255/.330/.457 line against southpaws is more than serviceable.
Despite having so many lefties in the lineup on a daily basis, the Yankees as a whole don't suffer much from it. The club is hitting a collective .247/.318/.422 against left-handed pitching this season, with a .740 OPS that ranks ninth. Remember, for most of that time, Aaron Judge hasn't been a factor, either.
Looking ahead, the Yankees' most likely opponent in the Wild Card series is the Red Sox, who are loaded with left-handers. In the rotation, they boast southpaws Payton Tolle and Ranger Suárez, with their being a possibility that Jake Bennett makes the cut, too. In the bullpen, they'll hope to unleash Garrett Crochet, Erik Miller and old friend Aroldis Chapman.
However, rather than being overmatched, we might say that this plays into the Yankees' hands. New York can handle left-handed pitching, and those lefty bats can tee off against righties. Jones emerging as a threat against southpaws only solidifies the strength and gives the Yankees another regular who doesn't need a platoon partner, allowing them to match up only where they're vulnerable.

ST. PETERSBURG -- While the Red Sox were engaged in a tough battle with the Rays on Saturday, losing 2-1, two of their rehabbing pitchers took steps forward.
Garrett Crochet, the lefty ace who is trying to make it back in time to serve as reliever in the postseason, threw another two-inning side session on Saturday, this one at Polar Park in Worcester, Mass.
If Crochet doesn’t have any ill effects coming out of that session, the Red Sox are hopeful they can have him face hitters at Fenway Park early next week, and perhaps multiple times in the team’s final homestand leading up to the postseason.
“I think it just depends on how he feels coming out of it, how much volume we give him,” said Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy. “So it's hard to say. I know it's not a great answer, but it's just really how it is. How does he feel after each step? So when he does that, how does he feel? And then determine from there. Do we give him more hitters or do we want to put him in a game? It’s hard to say until you know how he feels.”
Meanwhile, righty Tanner Houck made his final rehab appearance for Triple-A Worcester, allowing two hits and two runs (one earned) over 3 1/3 innings. Houck walked none and struck out two as he continued to make progress in his return from Tommy John surgery.
As is the case with Crochet, Houck doesn’t have time to build back up as a starter, but he could be a bullpen option for the Sox in October.
Perhaps Houck could make an appearance or two during the season-ending homestand against the Guardians and Cubs, which starts Tuesday.

There's a version of this continuous Boston Red Sox news saga that could have sent fans into a real panic, and I get why. Justin Slaten had quietly turned into one of the more trustworthy arms in this bullpen, working to a 2.84 ERA over his final two months of availability before elbow trouble sidelined him in August.
Now we know the full picture: an evaluation revealed degenerative changes in the flexor mass of his right elbow, and rather than push for a return with the postseason approaching, the Red Sox are having him get a PRP injection and start planning for 2027 instead.
On the year, he had thirty-six appearances, a 4.60 ERA overall, but provided a real chunk of high-leverage relief work, which is now gone for the stretch run. That's a real hole, absolutely. It's also not the whole story right now, and it's worth taking a breath before assuming the bullpen just got worse.
Garrett Crochet was the AL Cy Young runner-up last season, an 18-5, 2.59 ERA workhorse who threw 205.1 innings and struck out 255 batters. What a lot of people forget is that before all of that, Crochet broke into pro ball as a reliever with the Chicago White Sox, sitting comfortably in the upper 90s and regularly touching triple digits in short bursts. That's exactly the version the Red Sox may get back down the stretch.
He hasn't pitched in a game since throwing six scoreless innings on April 25, and after months sidelined with a shoulder issue that turned into more of a lingering problem, he just threw his first bullpen sessions in nearly three months. There isn't time left to stretch him back out as a starter, but a Crochet who can air it out for one to three innings at a time is exactly the profile that's thrived in October before.
Pair that with a Payton Tolle start going five or six innings, Crochet bridging the seventh and eighth, and Aroldis Chapman closing it out, and that's a real, dangerous alignment behind Sonny Gray in a Game 1.
Tanner Houck and Johan Oviedo are trending toward returns to Red Sox bullpen alongside Garrett Crochet
Crochet isn't walking through that door alone, either. Tanner Houck is further along than anyone, working back from UCL surgery and already up to three innings and 48 pitches in a rehab outing for Double-A Portland, allowing just one run with four strikeouts, before moving on to Triple-A Worcester to keep building and facing some better competition.
Johan Oviedo, who Boston acquired from the Pittsburgh Pirates over the winter, finally made his own rehab appearance with Worcester this week after missing more than five months with a flexor strain, which is a sign he could factor into the bullpen picture before the year is out. Kutter Crawford is the longer shot of the group, hasn't pitched for the big club since 2024, and there are only unconfirmed "rumblings" he could get a look at Worcester this week. Even if that goes nowhere in 2026, he's still under team control for two more seasons.
Losing Slaten hurts, and nobody should pretend otherwise. But between Crochet, Houck, and Oviedo all trending in the right direction at the same time, Boston may be walking into the stretch run with more usable, high-upside arms than it's had healthy at any single point all season.

ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — Willson Contreras stood at his locker Saturday afternoon and showed reporters the spot where a pitch hit his right hand in Texas on Thursday.
It was on the knuckles between his pinky finger and ring finger, and there was still swelling and a yellow bruise. Contreras could flex his hand but can’t yet grip a bat well enough to hit.
If you didn’t know Contreras was a baseball player, you’d think he was a boxer based on his battered hands.
“When I got hit, I felt my hand going numb. I thought it was bad because that’s a sign of a fracture,” he said. “That’s why I came off the game.”
Contreras is hopeful of getting in a few games before the start of the postseason.
“Hand’s still really sore. Woke up feeling a little better,” he said. “I can squeeze a little better than [Friday], but it’s gonna take a few days.”
The initial X-rays were negative, and any further scans will wait until after the swelling goes down, but Contreras is confident there isn’t a fracture based on his experience.
“I can squeeze a lot better. I’ve had fractures before, and when I have fractures, I couldn’t squeeze,” he said.
Contreras is hoping he can take some swings on Sunday. But because the injury is to his top hand, he has to make sure he can absorb the impact of making contact.
“I’m going to take it day-to-day. Of course I want to come back and play with the guys and be there for them,” he said. “It’s a part of baseball.”
Contreras said he might try using a guard over his batting glove to protect his hand.
The Sox play the Rays on Sunday afternoon and are off on Monday. Contreras could possibly return on Tuesday against the Guardians.
“I’m going to do everything in my power to get back on the field before the playoffs,” he said.
Contreras has been hit 24 times this season, tied for third-most in the majors, and 47 times over last two seasons. It’s largely because he stands close to the plate. But Contreras suggested on Thursday that Sox pitchers should retaliate on his behalf.
“I see, and completely feel and understand Willson’s frustration,” interim manager Chad Tracy said. “He’s been hit close to 50 times the last couple of years so he’s frustrated. Whether he’s referring to the umpires doing something or the pitchers, it’s irrelevant.”
Tracy acknowledged that Contreras crowds the plate. “But there’s a lot of guys that are close to the plate that don’t get hit as much as he does,” he said.
Rafaela progressing
Ceddanne Rafaela, who has been on the injured list since Sept. 3 with a strained right quadriceps, worked out at Worcester on Saturday and faced live pitching for the first time since the injury.
“I felt comfortable,” he said. “My body is rested, and I feel ready to go.”
The last hurdle is to sprint at 100 percent effort, something he will try on Sunday. Rafaela hopes to play against the Guardians on Tuesday.
Crochet could face hitters
Tracy said the goal set for Garrett Crochet would be to face hitters early in the week. That would likely be at Fenway Park before a game. Whether one such session would be enough to merit inclusion on the postseason roster isn’t certain. “Hard to say. I know that’s not a great answer, but it just really is,” Tracy said. … Righthanded reliever Tyron Guerrero could be activated off the injured list as soon as Sunday. He has been out since Sept. 1 with a sore shoulder.
Globe staff writer Alex Speier contributed to this report from Worcester.

Red Sox ace Crochet throws side session at Polar Park before WooSox game
WORCESTER — Garrett Crochet threw a baseball at Polar Park Saturday.
Four hours before the WooSox hosted the Durham Bulls (Tampa Bay Rays AAA club), the Red Sox star left-handed pitcher threw a side session as he continues his rehab from a left shoulder injury.
Crochet, dressed in a full white Red Sox uniform, tossed roughly 20 pitches and sat in the 91 to 92 mph range.
“He looks great,” WooSox pitching coach Dan DeLucia said. “It was pretty much what we expected. Like, that was the expectation, go out there and kind of make it an in-between side start. No, actually probably a tick above what I think the expectations were, but for the most part, as expected the fine-tuning things, getting on the mound again.
“(We had) one of the coaches stand in (in the batter’s box) and he still just needs to fine-tune things, and that takes some time, but the outputs look pretty good. Like, how the body’s moving and all that looks pretty good.”
Crochet (3-3, 6.30 ERA with 37 strikeouts in 30 IP) last pitched for the Red Sox on April 25 in a game against the Baltimore Orioles. He was placed on the 15-day injured list four days later (retroactive to April 26) and transferred to the 60-day IL on June 5.
While meeting with media members in St. Petersburg, Fla. Friday, Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy wasn’t clear on the next steps for Crochet moving forward as the Red Sox wrap up their regular season a week from Sunday.
Crochet is attempting to come back to help Boston out of the bullpen for their likely upcoming playoff series against the New York Yankees.
“It’s hard to say. If everything goes well Saturday, then you kind of determine what that looks like at the beginning part of next week,” said Tracy, according to Sean McAdam of MassLive. “I’d say we’re at a point where these next five days are going to be pretty telling. How does the side go and what can we do with him at the start of next week? That will give us a better idea.”
With fellow Red Sox pitcher Tanner Houck scheduled to pitch for Triple-A Worcester later in the day in a rehab assignment, both Crochet and Houck — and starting center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela, who hit living pitching at Polar Park pregame Saturday as he continues his recovery from a right quadriceps strain — present possible reinforcements for the Red Sox as they look to make a run in the playoffs.

With the New York Yankees likely to face off against the Boston Red Sox in the Wild Card Series, they will look to find any advantage they can to come out on top. That includes trying to gameplan against pitcher Payton Tolle, who will most likely be one of the Red Sox starters in the three-game set.
There's no question that Tolle is one the league's best and brightest young pitchers. Not only can he dominate a game, but he's so dang likeable that it's almost impossible to hate him. But that doesn't mean he's perfect.
Okay, he can be close to perfect sometimes, though. That's part of the problem. The Red Sox pitcher dazzled in the first inning in his Sept. 13 start against the Kansas City Royals. He threw the most smile-filled immaculate inning you’ll probably ever see, mainly utilizing his elite four-seam fastball. As his strongest pitch, he is using the four-seamer 45% of the time throughout his starts in 2026. And batters are hitting just .190 off of his heater on the season.
However, as the game against the Royals wore on, so did Tolle. His fastball velocity showed signs of dropping later in his start. While that's not too surprising for a starting pitcher, it could also be something for the Yankees to monitor. If they can work counts and force Tolle to throw a lot of pitches as he approaches a new and uncertain innings threshold, they may be able to sap his effectiveness early. The Royals start, as brilliant as it began, actually provided the Yankees with a blueprint.
The Yankees did not have luck against Tolle earlier this season
The Yankees are 1-1 against the Red Sox in games started by Tolle this season. However, he faced little resistance against the lineup in his two starts. On April 23, Tolle allowed just one run on three hits in six innings while striking out 11 batters. The Yankees scored three runs once Tolle left the game and picked up the win in Boston.
Two months later, Tolle pitched a seven-inning gem on June 26, once again at Fenway Park. He surrendered just one hit and two walks, striking out seven en route to a 6-1 Red Sox win. Nearly three months later, the Yankees will look to reverse their fortunes against the lefty. After a long season, the result could look a little differently for Tolle.
The 23-year-old has never thrown as many innings in a collegiate or professional season as he has in 2026. In fact, at 143 innings this season, he has pitched more than 50 innings over his previous career high. Now, you could look over at Cam Schlittler and say the thing, and you'd be correct. However, Schlittler’s velo hasn't trended downwards in a game as much as Tolle’s did on September 13.
To start the game, Tolle was consistently hitting 97 MPH with his four-seamer, a modest increase from his season average of 96.1 MPH. But by the sixth inning, his four-seam fastball was clocked as low as 92.7 MPH. Tolle still remained very effective, getting through the game without allowing a run and striking out seven. It's hard to say for certain if the wear and tear of a long MLB season is taking its toll on Tolle, but it could benefit a Yankees' lineup that has had mixed results against the fastball all season.
With an .845 slugging percentage against the heater, Ben Rice is by far the team's best batter when facing the cheese. He will look to set the tone early and jump on Tolle’s four-seamer. Luis García Jr. and Paul Goldschmidt have also raked against the fastball all season, though García Jr. has not hit as well against lefties. With Aaron Judge returning from injury and slowly returning to form, the team will have a decent advantage against any and all Red Sox fastballs, even Tolle's.
However, hitters like Cody Bellinger and Austin Wells will remain massive wild cards for the Yankees in the postseason. Each player has struggled to find success against the fastball in 2026. And if Jazz Chisholm Jr. is healthy enough to return to the lineup, his .338 slugging percentage will be the lowest of any starting position player. It'll be interesting to see which of these trends continues against Tolle’s fastball.
To add a hint of intrigue to the series, New York could also be facing off against another one of Boston's strong LHP. The Red Sox will gingerly work Garrett Crochet back into the mix, though he will also likely be on a pitch limit. It's not certain how the team will utilize Crochet, but he could certainly be a dangerous weapon for them, especially if paired with Tolle.
With Tolle already off to a great start in his career against the Yankees, he could continue his success this postseason. But with arm fatigue as a potential issue moving forward, his elite four-seam fastball may become just a little less overpowering. That's something that the Yankees could jump on.

In the absence of Shohei Ohtani and Aaron Judge, the mysterious power outages of Vlad Guerrero Jr. and Cal Raleigh, and the injuries to Tarik Skubal and Garrett Crochet, baseball’s postseason awards are coming into focus by ushering in a new wave of 20-something superstars.
Going into the weekend the teams with the best records in each league were the small market Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays, both of which with leading candidates for baseball’s postseason hardware who are still years away from their prime.
For the Brewers, 24-year-old Jacob Misiorowski is the runaway leader for the NL Cy Young Award, at 15-5 and leading the majors in ERA (1.89), strikeouts (243), WHIP (0.812) and strikeouts per nine innings (13.1) — while the Rays, in their bid to salt away the AL East, have gotten a late boost from their 23-year old third baseman Junior Caminero, who took over the AL home run lead last week and was neck and neck with Houston’s Yordan Alvarez in RBI and total bases.
On the surface, Alvarez, who leads the NL in OPS and batting (.311), would appear to have the overall statistical edge on Caminero for the MVP. But the fact that Alvarez is a DH and Caminero, who’s missed only one game while adding superior defense at third base for a team that is likely to win the division also bodes well for him. This is one race that figures to go down to the last day, with the deciding factor possibly being whether the Astros win the AL West.
As for the AL Cy Young Award, Cam Schlittler, the Yankees’ 25-year-old sophomore, has zoomed ahead of the Blue Jays’ Dylan Cease with a season for the ages, including a major league-leading 1.95 ERA and 0.904 WHIP and the most starts in Yankee history allowing one or fewer runs (21). His 1.14 ERA for 16 road starts is also the lowest in American League history.
Over in the National League, with Ohtani shackled with knee and bicep injuries that have prevented him from pitching since July 3, effectively ending his chances for a fourth straight MVP, the Cubs’ 24-year-old Pete Crow-Armstrong has stepped up with a phenomenal breakthrough season. Going into the weekend, Crow-Armstrong, who’s played every game, was leading the majors in slugging, OPS and total bases and was second behind Kyle Schwarber in the NL in homers with 44 and third in RBI with 105. On Aug. 29 he hit three homers in a game and with his 44th homer on Sept. 17 surpassed Hall of Famer Billy Williams as the most by a left-handed hitter in Cubs history.
Sorry, but we’re again unable to refrain from reminding that Crow-Armstrong was the Mets’ 2020 first round draft pick who, the next season, they traded to the Cubs for two months of rental free agent Javy Baez.
When it comes to the Rookies of the Year, I realize in this lost season for the Mets there’s been a lot of buzz for Nolan McLean and Carson Benge, but neither are going to win the NL award. That would have to be Cincinnati’s unsung Sal Stewart, who even if nobody probably had him on their Rookie of the Year bingo card at the start of the season, happens to be leading all NL rookies in homers (32) and RBI (110) and has played every day. An equally strong favorite for the AL Rookie of the Year is Cleveland lefty Parker Messick, a second round draft pick out of Florida State three years ago, who leads all AL rookies in wins (12), ERA (2.57), strikeouts (186) and WHIP (1.04).
IT’S A MADD, MADD WORLD
You have to wonder if the window has already closed on Aaron Judge leading the Yankees to a World Series title. The 34-year-old Yankee captain has missed 317 games (and counting) and had only four full seasons since 2018 and the fact remains he’s 280 pounds — and every time he has to make a diving catch or crash into a wall at his age now that’s 280 pounds of impact on his body. No surprise the rib injury that’s sidelined him most of this season. … For nine decades, Juan Vene was a fixture in the press boxes of Yankee Stadium and Shea Stadium and even though his name may not be familiar to most New York baseball fans, he was a legend, especially in his native Venezuela, but really all over Latin America. Word came last week that Vene passed away Sept. 15 in Miami at age 97. A long-time member of the Baseball Writers Association and a regular Hall of Fame voter, Vene was a friend to all of us. Anyone needing an interview with a Latin player in the offseason could count on Vene to help set it up. RIP. … If the White Sox are somehow able to hold on and win the AL Central it will be a remarkable achievement given the year-long state of their starting pitching. According to the Elias Bureau, White Sox starters have logged by far the fewest innings (639) in the majors to the runner-up Nationals’ 671 1/3, and as they stagger to the finish line they have been employing “openers” 2-3 times a week.

Boston Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy knows his team has figured out the Tampa Bay Rays pretty well this season.
That said, the Red Sox (84-70) still can learn more about the Rays (93-60) when the teams meet Saturday afternoon in St. Petersburg, Fla.
"At this point with (the Rays), we've played them enough already," Tracy said. "We have a pretty good understanding of them, (and) they have a pretty good understanding of us. But you could always pick up more stuff."
In Friday's series opener, the Red Sox scored four runs over the first three innings and won 4-2 to snap Tampa Bay's six-game winning streak and improve to 6-5 this season vs. the Rays.
Boston currently holds the second wild-card position in the American League but is dealing with several injuries.
"We have guys beat up that aren't here, and the hope is we get people healthy, and the roster could look even different a week from now than it does right now," Tracy said.
Boston's Willson Contreras is day-to-day after getting hit on the hand, while closer Aroldis Chapman (lat tightness) has been unavailable the past two contests.
Right-hander Tanner Houck (Tommy John surgery in 2025) and lefty Garrett Crochet (left shoulder inflammation) have advanced in their rehab assignments.
Boston left-hander Payton Tolle (9-6, 3.02 ERA) is expected to make his 26th start on Saturday and will try to record his sixth consecutive win.
Tolle is 1-0 with an 0.75 ERA over 12 innings in his last two starts, allowing one run on eight hits while striking out 19 with a walk. He is 0-2 with a 4.50 ERA in two starts and one relief outing against Tampa Bay, which already has clinched a playoff berth.
Whatever Rays pitching coach Kyle Snyder and the rest of the staff have done with trade-deadline acquisition Freddy Peralta certainly has been a success.
Acquired by the club from the New York Mets for three prospects on Aug. 2, Peralta (9-11, 4.67 ERA) -- a right-hander who will start for the Rays on Saturday -- arrived from the Big Apple as a lesser version of what he was during his two All-Star seasons with the Milwaukee Brewers.
He was 5-9 with a 4.99 ERA with the Mets, but the work was immediately put in by the Rays to adjust Peralta to where he was when he was a 17-game winner with a sub-3.00 ERA last season.
"For some reason, when I got here, when I sat here with Kyle and (bullpen coach Jorge Moncada) and (manager Kevin Cash), they told me, like, 'You're gonna do what you want to do here, and we are going to help you to do it,'" Peralta said.
"And we know what you need to do to make those adjustments. We just put everything on the table. I just followed all the instructions, and it's what I am right now."
With the Rays, Peralta is 4-2 with a 3.86 ERA in eight starts, but his past four outings have been gems. He has pitched 23 innings and has allowed just two runs on 10 hits, with 17 strikeouts, four walks and an 0.78 ERA in that span.
"Fastball Freddy," who is using his changeup much more with the Rays, is 0-2 with a 5.40 ERA in three career starts against Boston.
Peralta allowed two runs on three hits in 4 1/3 innings in a 4-0 loss at Boston on July 11 while with the Mets.

ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — A year ago, as the Red Sox crept toward the end of the regular season, the pitching choices for their looming Wild Card Series in New York were limited. Beyond ace Garrett Crochet, who dominated the Yankees in Game 1, the Red Sox ended up going with the unreliable Brayan Bello in Game 2 and the untested Connelly Early in Game 3. Two losses later, they were packing their bags for the winter.
This year, with a replay of that series feeling all but certain to begin a week from Tuesday and once again in the Bronx, the pitching plans look nothing like they did back then.
Which is good news for the Red Sox.
Even with Crochet sidelined all season by injury, the pitching rotation has been, in the words of interim manager Chad Tracy, “pivotal” to the drastic midseason turnaround that lifted this team from the depths of the American League standings and into the playoff race.
A trade for Sonny Gray. The continued development of Payton Tolle. And the free agent signing of Ranger Suarez. Three big moves, three likely starters for one more entry in the ongoing Boston/New York postseason clash of baseball titans.
Friday night in Florida, it was Suarez’s turn to prove his readiness. Facing the first-place Rays presented an obvious test, but for Suarez, it also was a chance to build on his two previous starts, in which he allowed only one run in 14 innings. As Tracy pointed out before the game, there is no mystery into what makes a good Suarez outing. Control the tempo, get ahead in the count, and locate pitches. When the lefthander does those three things, he can be pretty hard to beat.
But, as the Rays learned Friday, even if he doesn’t quite do those three things as well as he wants to, he can still find a way to battle through.
So there he was at the end of a decidedly mixed bag of a night, leading the Sox to a 4-2 win, improving his record to 8-4 after giving up just one run in 5⅔ innings. On the upside, he struck out five and consistently got key outs in key moments.
On the downside, he had to labor mightily to get there, walking a career-high five batters, throwing just 56 of his 98 pitches for strikes. He got away with it this time, but come the playoffs, that’s playing with fire, whether against the Yankees or perhaps the Rays again, with Tampa Bay in line to host the wild-card winners.
The Sox chose to take the positive out of the night.
“When I issued those walks, I think that the game was taking me to a place that wasn’t the right one. So I just tried to take a deep breath and slow it down, and I was able to then take it from there,” Suarez said.
He struck out Yandy Díaz to end the second inning, stranding two runners on base. He got out of another jam in the third, a Chandler Simpson hard-hit line out to right and a strikeout of Jonny DeLuca to strand two more runners.
Suarez did it again in the fourth, helping his own cause by starting a nifty inning-ending double play, snaring Taylor Walls’s line drive to the mound and then throwing to first to double off Nick Fortes.
A clean fifth ended on a called third strike to Junior Caminero, but gave way to a messier sixth, with a leadoff walk to Ryan Vilade eventually leading Tracy to pull the plug as Suarez approached 100 pitches. But not before he struck out DeLuca to get the first out.
“He’s a very good competitor and a really good pitcher,” Tracy said, “that even when he’s got traffic, you trust that he’s going to find his way through it. . . . He walked five, but still almost completed six innings. He was very competitive with men on base.”
“I got traffic every single inning because of the walks, but I was able to limit damage today, and that was part of it,” Suarez said. “It was one of those nights that you didn’t have the command, but I was able to turn the page quickly and was able to get outs when I needed.”
Good as the escape act was, it’s all just staging for what comes next, a playoff berth the Red Sox could clinch on Saturday. Suarez was signed in part because of his experience in the postseason, earned across eight seasons with the Phillies. Suarez is 4-1 with a 1.48 ERA in 11 playoff appearances, which includes eight starts. He was the winner of Game 3 of the 2022 World Series, beating the eventual champion Astros with five shutout innings.
The Phillies also called on him to come out of the bullpen in Game 5 of the NLCS, and all he did was earn his first postseason save by getting two outs on two pitches, stranding the winning run and clinching the Series berth.
“When you get to this part of the season, not every outing is going to go perfectly. But he’s been there and done that as far as navigating his way through an outing and finding a way to strand base runners,” Tracy said. “The game’s not going to speed up on him. You know, even if he’s walked some and there’s some people on base, he doesn’t ever look like he speeds up. He just keeps making his pitches.”
Tara Sullivan is a Globe columnist. She can be reached at tara.sullivan@globe.com. Follow her @Globe_Tara.

ST. PETERSBURG – As they head into the final 10 days of the regular season, the Red Sox are monitoring a plethora of injuries to key players.
Given that the Sox still hold firm possession of the second American League Wild Card spot and could clinch a berth as early as this weekend, the plan will be to operate conservatively in hopes of getting everyone healthy for the games that count the most.
Here is an update on where things stand with those key players.
First baseman Willson Contreras
There was a big scare on Thursday night in Texas when the team’s most productive hitter this season was pelted on the top of his right hand with a pitch in the top of the eighth and immediately exited the game. Contreras said that in the moment, it felt like a fracture. Fortunately, X-rays taken at the ballpark were negative.
While interim manager Chad Tracy mentioned the possibility of follow-up imaging, there was none on Friday. Contreras didn’t have his hand taped and spent his share of time in the training room.
Where do things stand?
“Obviously, sore with some swelling,” Tracy said. “So nothing new other than just over the next couple of days, they'll work on treatment, on getting the swelling out, see if he can get grip strength back, and then we'll go from there. So just day to day.”
Could there still be additional scans?
“Not right now. Right now, with the initial one, they're optimistic,” said Tracy. “Just work on the swelling and see how he progresses over the next couple days, and then determine if they feel like they need more. But right now, they're just going to work on that.”
Closer Aroldis Chapman
When Garrett Whitlock closed Thursday’s win in Texas, it was obvious something was up with Chapman. It turns out he has been dealing with lat tightness he sustained while working out prior to Tuesday’s game.
Chapman downplayed the injury on Friday, saying the team is being conservative and that he felt healthy enough to play catch before the opener of the three-game series against the Rays. The Red Sox told him not to.
The lefty fireballer said he won’t pitch this weekend, but he expects to return during the final homestand, which starts on Tuesday.
“I’m not worried at all,” Chapman said. “From the first time I felt it to today, I feel very good. I was going to go out and throw, but the team wants to take it slow, and they want me to take my time.“
It is all about being 100% for the first game of the playoffs on Sept. 29, right?
“Yeah, of course,” said Chapman. “A hundred percent.”
Center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela
Boston’s All-Star center fielder hasn’t played since Sept. 2 due to a right quad strain. It sounds unlikely he’ll be able to play in a rehab game for Triple-A Worcester because that season ends on Sunday. But Tracy is confident with where Rafaela is at.
“I think he got close to 90% of his acceleration yesterday,” said Tracy. “So not ready yet, but he's moving quickly in the right direction, which is good. If he doesn’t play [for Worcester], there is a goal of getting him some live at-bats of some kind. You know, like live BP-type at-bats of some kind, plus the Trajekt. The important thing is that the running piece keeps going in the right direction.”
Left-hander Garrett Crochet
Boston’s ace, who has been out since April 25 due to a left shoulder injury, is still racing against the clock to try to pitch in relief during the postseason. His next step will be on Saturday, when he throws his second up-and-down bullpen session of the week at Fenway Park.
For Crochet to have any shot at pitching at the start of the postseason, he would have to start facing hitters by next week.
“I would say we're to the point where these next five days or so are going to be pretty telling,” said Tracy. “How does the side go, and what can we do with him early next week? And that'll give us a better idea of the answer to that question.”
Right-hander Tanner Houck
The righty will make the fourth and final appearance of his Minor League rehab assignment when he throws roughly 50 pitches for Worcester on Saturday. It’s possible Houck will get a tuneup or two in regular-season action for the Red Sox next week, which could give the club a better gauge if he’s a possibility to pitch in the playoffs. Houck had Tommy John surgery 13 months ago.

Contreras is out of the lineup for Friday's series opener.

According to WEEI's Rob Bradford, Crochet will throw another side session on Saturday as he continues to work his way back from left shoulder inflammation that has kept him out since April 29.
After turning to Garrett Whitlock to lock down Thursday's win, Tracy told reporters, including Cotillo, that Chapman was unavailable with LAT tightness. According to Bradford, Chapman said the injury popped up ahead of Tuesday's series opener in Texas and that he wasn't concerned about the injury, saying the latest he would return to the mound would be during the team's upcoming home stand, beginning on Tuesday night, if he doesn't make an appearance in Tampa.
Tyron Guerrero
After landing on the injured list on Sept. 1 with right shoulder inflammation. The 35-year-old flamethrower was expected to be activated when he was first eligible, ahead of Wednesday's game in Texas. However, after experiencing lower back tightness, the team delayed his activation. According to Bradford, Guerrero "felt fine" after throwing 20 pitches off the mound on Friday afternoon. However, it still remains unclear when he may be activated.
The 32-year-old outfielder landed on the injured list last Friday with a "right foot ligament injury" after getting it caught in the grates along the center field wall in the Sept. 8 loss to the Los Angeles Angels. As Bradford noted, White has been diagnosed with a ligament tear, likely ending his season.
White's injury seems to open the door for Spring Training standout Braiden Ward to join the Red Sox as a fourth outfielder/pinch runner in the playoffs.
